newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed to offer solution to NATO row.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed to offer solution to NATO row.

text.p: Russia's controversial security chief Alexander Lebed set foot on Western soil for the first time on Sunday, saying he had proposals to end a dispute with NATO over alliance plans to expand eastwards.

The former paratroop general, on a two-day visit to the NATO headquarters that for two decades of his army career was the "lion's den", said on arrival in Brussels he sought a civilised dialogue with alliance chief Javier Solana.

"Yes, there are some new proposals, but first of all they are intended for the ears of Mr Solana," he said in the low growling voice that served him well in his army service and seems to do him no harm in his new political career.
Lebed walked down the steps of his airliner wrapped in a tight black trenchcoat despite blue skies and warm Brussels sunshine. At his side was his red-headed wife of 25 years, Inna.
Asked how he felt on arriving in the West for the first time, the 46-year-old former paratrooper remained stony-faced.
"I have no special feelings. I feel comfortable wherever I am, including the West."
Lebed, who meets NATO Secretary-General Solana on Monday, said he would be seeking first-hand information about the alliance's aims in embracing former Kremlin alies such as Poland.
The curiosity will be strong on both sides.
Lebed's visit is his first beyond the borders of the former Soviet Union, apart from his service in Moscow's ill-fated Afghan campaign.

Since his political breakthrough in the summer's presidential election, his robust political style and sometimes contradictory statements have left some Western officials with more questions than answers. He has, however, made one thing abundantly clear: that he intends one day to become president.
Boris Yeltsin's approaching heart surgery adds another element to the visit. While Yeltsin is incapacitated, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin assumes presidential powers.
But should Yeltsin fail to return to duties, Lebed would be a strong contender in new elections.

The president himself has fluctuated in his enthusiasm for the four-star general, hinting one moment that he saw him as his heir and slapping him down the next. He also has enemies in the security apparatus and government.
Lebed, talking to journalists at Brussels airport, said he had been misunderstood in the West.

"Some commentators of ill-will have been saying that Lebed is threatening NATO with nuclear weapons, and saying Russia is ready to occupy some of these countries (applying for NATO membership) if there is the slightest move of NATO to the east.
"These are the worst fairy tales of the Cold War," he said.
He described the situation in Afghanistan, where militant Taleban Islamic militia have seized power, as very serious but declined to say whether he would discuss it with Solana.
He said he feared efforts to annex parts of the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan to Afghanistan.
Russia sees Afghanistan's border with Tajikistan as the frontline of its sphere of influence and keeps thousands of troops there.

While Lebed acted quickly under Yeltsin's orders to end conflict with separatist Islamic rebels in Russia's breakaway Chechen region -- his most courageous political action since being drafted into the administration -- he has shown markedly more wariness of the Taleban.
